idiom_name: empty trait mixed into classes, tested with isInstanceOf or a bound
implementation_notes: Scala traits may be empty and the standard library uses the pattern - scala.Serializable, and Scala 3's scala.CanEqual, documented as 'a marker trait indicating that values of type L can be compared to values of type R'. Mix a marker trait into a class and test with isInstanceOf or a type bound. Scala's modern idiom prefers sealed traits/enums for closed sets and given-based type classes for open capabilities, so reserve plain markers for facts genuinely intrinsic to the type; because a marker trait can extend another trait, categories compose.
code_sketch:
trait Deletable                 // empty marker

final class Order extends Deletable

def purge[A <: Deletable](xs: List[A]): Unit = ()
val marked: Boolean = order.isInstanceOf[Deletable]
pitfalls: The mark is inherited for good: a subclass cannot opt out of the trait.
isInstanceOf is erased for parameterized types, so markers with type parameters need a TypeTest or ClassTag.
Keep marker traits free of fields and initialization logic or mixin linearization order starts to matter.

variants.name: Sealed trait or enum tag for a closed set
variants.idiom_name: Scala 3 enum / sealed trait with exhaustive match
variants.implementation_notes: Scala 3 enums and sealed traits give the compiler the complete set of cases, so a marker whose real purpose is enumeration becomes a sealed hierarchy checked by exhaustive match - no runtime test and no empty interface. Use it for closed categories inside a codebase; keep a plain marker trait for categories that other modules must be able to join. The refactor direction is one-way: an open marker that becomes closed should become sealed.
variants.code_sketch:
enum Primitive:
  case Text(value: String)
  case Num(value: Int)

def render(p: Primitive): String = p match
  case Primitive.Text(v) => v
  case Primitive.Num(n)  => n.toString
pitfalls: Sealed hierarchies require implementations in the same source file (Scala 3 enums) or compilation unit, which constrains module layout.
Exhaustivity warnings become errors under -Xfatal-warnings and can block adding a case until every match is updated.
Enums cannot extend classes, so an existing class hierarchy may not be convertible to the sealed model.

variants.name: Marker type class with given instances (CanEqual style)
variants.idiom_name: marker trait summoned as a given context parameter
variants.implementation_notes: Scala 3's CanEqual shows the functional refinement: a marker trait with no members, summoned as a given and taken as a context parameter, so the mark participates in type checking without any runtime representation, and the compiler can refuse operations for unmarked type combinations. Use it when the mark is a compile-time permission rather than a nominal subtype - especially when it must not be inherited implicitly by subclasses. The pattern adds a type-class layer instead of a supertype, so marked types need no modification.
pitfalls: Given instances are resolved by scope and implicit priority; a stray instance silently grants the mark.
There is no runtime test for the marker - reflection-based frameworks cannot see it.
A universal fallback instance (the canEqualAny trap) makes the marker permissive unless strict mode or precise scopes prevent it.
